pull.title: script: store interpreter stack elements as reference-counted objects
pull.body:
Modifies the script interpreter to represent stack elements internally using smart pointers, making duplication memory-cheap, and giving us caching keys which are cheap and guaranteed unique by the compiler. First part of a 2-part project to improve script interpreter performance in preparation for PQ signatures. 

No consensus changes - a pure performance improvement refactor.

## Motivation 

We presently have `MAX_SCRIPT_ELEMENT_SIZE = 520`, but in the near future, motivated by the need for PQ signature schemes, we may want to introduce soft fork changes which increase the max stack element size for new output types well into the multi-kilobyte range. This may be perhaps as high as 10kb or more given the current landscape of PQ signature schemes' sizes. 

Ongoing related work:

- https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/blob/main/leaf-version-0xC2.mediawiki#user-content-Relaxing_the_Max_Stack_Element_Size
- https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/pull/76

This poses a new problem to today's implementations if deployed naively. 

Today's Bitcoin script interpreter moves around raw mutable byte vectors to represent stack elements. When those elements are duplicated, the underlying byte vectors are deep-copied. When hash opcodes execute, they always invoke the corresponding hash function and fully ingest the top stack element. Duplication and hashing cost only a single weight unit in tapscript, with no upper limit on how many times they can be executed, aside from implicit limits due to the 10,000 byte script size maximum.

If we were to simply up the stack element size limit from 520b to 10kb, then we exacerbate an existing DoS vector on bitcoin nodes: Push a big (today 520b, maybe someday 10kb) stack element, then duplicate and hash it over and over. Worst case would be a script like this:

```cpp
<big_blob> DUP DUP [DUP3 RMD160 DROP RMD160 DROP RMD160 DROP]...
```  

...with the `[...]` part repeating up to the script size limit. RMD160 is used because it lacks hardware acceleration support and so performs significantly worse than even HASH256 or HASH160, making a more effective CPU attack.

This costs the attacker only \~20000 weight units (10kb for the script, 10kb for the stack element), but forces all validators to evaluate OP_RIPEMD160 about 4284 times, each on the same 10kb input. That's about 672588 RMD160 compressions in software.

I ran a benchmark (not in this PR) using this style of script with 520b and 10kb script elements. 

- 520b: validation takes about **3 milliseconds**
- 10,000b: validation takes about **52 milliseconds**

## This PR

(idea credit: EthanHeilman)

To address this risk, we would want to implement a **hash cache** for all the hashing opcodes. However, to implement such a cache safely in consensus, we need extremely robust cache keys. A collision in the cache key would be a consensus bug because the cache would return the wrong hash for a given input. But we can't cryptographically hash the inputs to compute a cache key... that is the same work we are trying to avoid with the cache. 

Instead we can kill two birds with two PRs. 

1. Replace stack elements with ref-counting pointers, so OP_DUP et al duplicate pointers and not the underlying raw bytes. :arrow_backward:  **THIS PR**
2. Implement a hash cache keyed by the stack element pointers. Each cache entry holds a handle to the key pointer so that the key doesn't get dropped and the pointer reallocated for a new stack element (which would cause a consensus bug). Cache key uniqueness is guaranteed by the compiler.  :arrow_backward: **Future PR**

Stage 1 reduces the asymmetric memory inflation attack allowed by OP_DUP et al. Stage 2 fixes the asymmetric CPU DoS attack. To be clear, neither stage fully prevents an attacker from uploading a series of large stack elements, and duplicating/hashing them. But we **do** force attackers to pay for those operations with fees and block space. 

I have both stage 1 and 2 implemented locally and can show benchmarks to prove the effect of the cache, if desired. I could have submitted it all as one PR but both stages are atomic and could do well with separate review.

I looked at this issue in the past and concluded it wasn't worth the effort, but from the angle of increasing the max stack element size, it does become an attack vector.

Did you benchmark the cost of making the inner vector a shared pointer for current regular scripts? I'd expect it to be slightly worse.

I think we can do better by turning the stack element into a standalone class that is either a prevector or a `std::shared_ptr<std::vector>` depending on the element's size. That should be more efficient than the status quo for small elements and no worse for regular scripts, while keeping cheap duplication for large ones.

Also, my agent and Ralph (https://git.fish.foo/bitcoin/bitcoin/pulls/36721#issuecomment-619311) flagged potential contention on the shared shared_ptr reference count might be worth looking at under parallel validation context.
Please fold the fixups back or turn it into a draft to signal that it's not ready for review yet

> Did you benchmark the cost of making the inner vector a shared pointer for current regular scripts? I'd expect it to be slightly worse.

@ismaelsadeeq I used the existing benchmarks and the delta is negligible or better for regular scripts. The only one meaningfully worsened by this PR is `VerifyNestedIfScript` due to the number of pushes, leading to a +38% slowdown on that benchmark, but we're talking about a difference of a few nanoseconds per push (on my machine). But that script doesn't seem like a good representative for an adversarial attack _or_ for a common happy path. If an attacker wanted to waste CPU time, they'd use hashing opcodes, which are far slower than push opcodes like `OP_1`, or of course checksig opcodes. If he wanted to consume memory, he'd use OP_DUP.

| Benchmark | Before | After | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| VerifyNestedIfScript | 11,140 ns | 15,459 ns | +38.8% |
| VerifyScriptP2WPKH | 20,102 ns | 21,573 ns | +7.3% |
| VerifyScriptP2TR_KeyPath | 21,424 ns | 20,435 ns | -4.6% |
| VerifyScriptP2TR_ScriptPath | 38,347 ns | 36,244 ns | -5.5% |

run-to-run noise on my machine seems to be +/- 7%, so everything but `VerifyNestedIfScript` was well within that. 

I did not go so far as to write any new benchmarks, but I will try to hammer some together that better demonstrate the costs this PR introduces.

> I think we can do better by turning the stack element into a standalone class that is either a prevector or a std::shared_ptr<std::vector> depending on the element's size. That should be more efficient than the status quo for small elements and no worse for regular scripts, while keeping cheap duplication for large ones.

Neat idea. In my current stage 2 impl, the hash cache has a minimum input size needed to trigger it (currently set to 128 bytes). If we arrange so that the prevector's small-buffer size limit matches the hash cache minimum threshold, then we'd never hit the prevector's small-buffer size limit. Add in the fact that stack elements are never grown, so their size is fixed at constructor time. So we could have a `ScriptStackElem` as a struct which embeds a union of `char[127]` and `struct { char* indirect; size_type capacity }`. Any value smaller than 128 bytes would fit in the statically allocated array. Any value larger would go to the heap.

Is that worth the complexity in consensus-critical code though? the benchmarks don't seem to indicate any major issues with the present design. @Yudis-bit did find benchmarks that slowed down, but i need to see how he got those numbers first before i can figure out why.

> The only one meaningfully worsened by this PR is VerifyNestedIfScript … a few nanoseconds per push

Yeah, I was just after the numbers. Signature verification dominates the interpreter today, so per-push cost is noise. But that's an artifact of where the cost sits right now, not a permanent property: if sigop verification moves off the hot path — batched or offloaded (e.g. to a GPU), with optimistic script execution that defers the actual signature checks and only fails later if one doesn't verify — then stack-op work becomes the dominant interpreter cost, and a few ns per push starts to matter. So the +38% on pushes isn't irrelevant forever; it's just hidden behind ECDSA/Schnorr for now.

> I will try to hammer some [benchmarks] together…

Nice, curious to see them.

> ScriptStackElem as a struct … union of char[127] and { char* indirect; size_type capacity }

Really like this.

> Is that worth the complexity in consensus-critical code though?

Yep, thin motivation while the underlying proposal is speculative. But it's a nice problem to brainstorm, and if we're doing the refactor anyway, doing the more optimal change is better for me.

Another potential direction is to have the (proposed sigop) opcode read from multiple stack elements instead of one. Then the signature stays as ≤520-byte chunks and gets streamed into the verifier, and we never raise the element-size limit at all,  so the large-element attack surface is never opened in the first place.

@ismaelsadeeq Benchmarks pushed. I added them as earlier commits so they can be tested with or without the `ScriptStackElem` changes. 

| Benchmark Name | Before (ns) | After (ns) | Delta |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| VerifyScriptP2SH_P2WPKH | 21,328 | 21,387 | +0.3% |
| VerifyPushDropSmall | 52,119 | 81,063 | +55.5% |
| VerifyDupDropLarge | 108,646 | 48,862 | -55.0% |

So basically it seems like this change makes simple data pushing slower, but makes duplication much cheaper. I will look into the union type idea and see whether that improves the situation at all.

> Another potential direction is to have the (proposed sigop) opcode read from multiple stack elements instead of one. Then the signature stays as ≤520-byte chunks and gets streamed into the verifier, and we never raise the element-size limit at all, so the large-element attack surface is never opened in the first place.

We did consider this type of chunking as an option. Ultimately this would be a trade-off that passes complexity down to wallet developers and users. This gets especially hairy when we consider that some signature algorithms like SHRINCS have variable-size signatures. So we decided against this route, [full explanation here](https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/blob/4fe68e3a68fd58be6b0e19436ff6fb7a3357a291/leaf-version-0xC2.mediawiki#user-content-Relaxing_the_Max_Stack_Element_Size)

after some experimenting with the union-based approach, i could not make it perform meaningfully better than a simple intrusive ref-counter which seemed much less error-prone. [Experimental intrusive ref-counting code pushed to this branch](https://github.com/conduition/bitcoin/compare/scriptvalptr-stage1..scriptvalptr-stage1-refctr). It achieves performance at or better than `master` on these benchmarks. 

| Benchmark | 104c7a02 | `scriptvalptr-stage1` (8b9ef52a) | `scriptvalptr-stage1-refctr` (ad6cef8b2) |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| VerifyScriptP2WPKH | 20133 | 20373 | 20432 |
| VerifyScriptP2SH_P2WPKH | 21357 | 21263 | 20741 |
| VerifyScriptP2TR_KeyPath | 20454 | 20283 | 20433 |
| VerifyScriptP2TR_ScriptPath | 36100 | 36069 | 36621 |
| VerifyNestedIfScript | 11592 | 15890 | 9938 |
| VerifyPushDropSmall | 55154 | 85622 | 48993 |
| VerifyDupDropLarge | 110920 | 49964 | 38022 |
| VerifyPushDropSized8 | 1823 | 2575 | 1853 |
| VerifyPushDropSized24 | 2124 | 2825 | 2114 |
| VerifyPushDropSized40 | 2444 | 3236 | 2414 |
| VerifyPushDropSized56 | 2735 | 3477 | 2715 |
| VerifyPushDropSized520 | 2765 | 2906 | 2706 |

The cost of course is the greater impl complexity, using a homebrewed pointer type to handle stack elements is risky. If you think the performance is worth it, i'll update this PR branch.

EDIT: updated with additional benchmarks

> We did consider this type of chunking as an option. Ultimately this would be a trade-off that passes complexity down to wallet developers and users. This gets especially hairy when we consider that some signature algorithms like SHRINCS have variable-size signatures. So we decided against this route, [full explanation here](https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/blob/4fe68e3a68fd58be6b0e19436ff6fb7a3357a291/leaf-version-0xC2.mediawiki#user-content-Relaxing_the_Max_Stack_Element_Size)

I started reading the proposal, and the branching inside `OP_CHECKSIG` on whether the signature is stateful or stateless feels a bit icky; those are two different schemes, and bundling them into one leaf checksig is where some of the complexity comes from?

I think it'd be better to split them into separate BIPs for stateful SHRINCS and stateless SHRINCS, and commit both as leaves in a taproot tree. Then which scheme runs is decided by the leaf you reveal, not by checking the signature mid-opcode eval. (I'd recommend this even if we end up increasing the script element size.)

On the variable-size point from [full explanation here](https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/blob/4fe68e3a68fd58be6b0e19436ff6fb7a3357a291/leaf-version-0xC2.mediawiki#user-content-Relaxing_the_Max_Stack_Element_Size), splitting actually makes it okayish. The stateless leaf is fixed-size, a fixed n-element read, no decisions. The stateful leaf is variable, and we can do like a self-delimiting read, read chunks into the verifier, which already has the length from an indicator byte in the first chunk, and stop once it has that many bytes capped at a max. 
This way, no spender supplied count, the stop comes from the signature's own (verified) length, so a lie just fails, and the cap means a garbage indicator byte can at worst make you read n elements. Statically then "this opcode pops ≤n, known from the leaf".

(You could instead pad to a fixed n for the stateful leaf with empties to make the pop count constant, but that's a bit of a hack) I think this is a far smaller thing to reason about than multi-KB elements across the whole interpreter (it has a wider scope).

I think this is ideally the same with the current version of the shrincs proposal?,  both leaves under one output are still one address that can always spend, stateful or stateless.



re: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36721#issuecomment-6624074329

Nice benchmarks, thanks for the results.

> I started reading the proposal, and the branching inside OP_CHECKSIG on whether the signature is stateful or stateless feels a bit icky; those are two different schemes, and bundling them into one leaf checksig is where some of the complexity comes from?

i should disambiguate here: the multiplexed OP_CHECKSIG defined in that BIP is designed to deploy new signature algorithms like SHRINCS, or maybe someday SQIsign/Falcon/whatever. That BIP doesn't know anything about the stateful vs stateless signing components in SHRINCS. It treats every signature scheme as a black box verification subroutine that takes a triple of byte strings in, and returns success/fail. SHRINCS is defined as one single unified signature scheme within that framework. I should also mention [that BIP is presently being rewritten, to remove SHRINCS-specific language](https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/pull/76)

SHRINCS' verification subroutine does indeed branch based on the signature's leading 'indicator' byte - that is a hard requirement to achieve its design properties. But to the script interpreter, that branching is completely black-box. It is not part of script. 

If we chunked signatures into 520b elements though, and relied on the signature itself to tell us how many chunks to pop, we could not use SHRINCS (or any variable-size signature scheme, for that matter) as a black box anymore. Increasing the stack element size limit allows us to keep that black-box compatibility with any signature scheme up to the new size limit.

[Here is the current `shrincs_verify` reference code](https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/blob/4fe68e3a68fd58be6b0e19436ff6fb7a3357a291/SHRINCS.md#shrincs_verify) in case you're interested. 

> I think it'd be better to split them into separate BIPs for stateful SHRINCS and stateless SHRINCS, and commit both as leaves in a taproot tree. Then which scheme runs is decided by the leaf you reveal, not by checking the signature mid-opcode eval. (I'd recommend this even if we end up increasing the script element size.)

We did consider a design where the stateful and stateless components are entirely separate schemes, whose keys can be stashed in disjoint tapscript leaves. However this would severely complicate scripting. Think about how you'd design a 2-of-3 multisig output, where each signer has two possible keys they may use, and we don't know which one they'll use until signing time. Every pubkey would need IF/ELSE branching, and every signature would need a true/false decision push (e.g. you sign stateless, i sign stateful, and vice versa, would use completely different pubkeys under this paradigm).

events.message:
script: remove the overload wrapper around EvalScript

Fold the two EvalScript declarations into a single one by defaulting the
ScriptExecutionData argument, so a caller with no execution data to pass simply
omits it instead of going through an overload wrapper.

Callers that pass a ScriptError pointer must give a nullptr in this position,
and the two fuzz targets that passed a bare nullptr drop the argument entirely.
This is pure refactoring with no behaviour change.
tests: add benchmark for P2SH-wrapped P2WPKH script validation
tests: add benchmarks for stack pushing

script: store interpreter stack elements as reference-counted objects

The interpreter holds each stack item by value, so every opcode that
duplicates or reorders items copies their contents. A future output type
may soon raise the maximum stack element size well past today's 520 bytes,
at which point a few weight units of script would be enough to drive
megabytes of interpreter memory.

Store the items as reference-counted objects instead: each element is
materialized once per execution and shared from then on, and each gains a
stable identity that later work can use as keys for caching. Every caller
of the interpreter uses the new stack type. Opcode semantics unchanged.

script: test element sharing on the interpreter stack

Add unit tests for the interpreter's reference-counted stack: that duplicating and
reordering stack items share a single element rather than copying it, and that an
element is released once no stack slot holds it any more. No behaviour changes.

events.body: Fixed IWYU CI (and figured out how to run the CI on my own fork)

> It treats every signature scheme as a black box … SHRINCS is one single unified scheme within that framework.

Clearer, thanks. I think  https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/pull/76 approach is better, the leaf-version spec becomes a generic sig check, with each scheme defined in its own BIP. That makes the black-box boundary explicit, which is what I was missing.
So scheme choice stays committed per key/leaf (the flag lives in the pubkey). With that rewrite reserving `0x01` and moving SHRINCS out to its own BIP/flag, a scheme-flagged pubkey locks that spending path to that scheme, and only new outputs adopt future schemes. Is that the intended upgrade hook?

> SHRINCS branches on the indicator byte … but to the interpreter that branching is completely black-box.

Cool, the pubkey flag picks the scheme (e.g. SHRINCS vs BIP340), and within SHRINCS the indicator byte picks stateful vs stateless. From the interpreter's side, it's one indivisible unit; it never looks inside the sig. Makes sense.

> Increasing the stack element size limit keeps black-box compatibility up to the new size limit.

Alternative that keeps black-box *without* raising the limit: the pubkey flag already tells you the scheme, so you can bound the max pop count up front (for SHRINCS). For the exact count, `OP_CHECKSIG` pops the pubkey and the first chunk, then lets the verifier read the indicator byte and say how many more chunks it needs, pops them, and verifies the concatenation. The interpreter never parses the sig itself, the verifier returns an opaque, bounded count, so it stays black-box; the signature just arrives as ≤520-byte pieces. (Inspired by https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/issues/3#issuecomment-4918125246.) And when you add a new flag the max can be adapted as well?

If we do raise the script element size: keeping the 1000-items stack limit means the total stack-data ceiling goes up by a lot. Do you plan to pair that with a lower max stack element count or a max stack bytes budget too?

> … separate stateful/stateless schemes would severely complicate scripting.

Indeed, doesn't work for multisig on one pubkey. The two independent leaves in a tree will not play well.

> Increasing the stack element size limit keeps black-box compatibility up to the new size limit.

Will await others to chime in and also follow the development. Not sure about https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/blob/4fe68e3a68fd58be6b0e19436ff6fb7a3357a291/leaf-version-0xC2.mediawiki#user-content-Relaxing_the_Max_Stack_Element_Size, still leaning towards the chunking idea.

I believe the problem this PR is trying to solve is better addressed at the consensus rule level. This refactoring might still be desirable, but it should be motivated independently of a possible soft fork.

If a proposed consensus change introduces a DoS vector by lifting a limit, the first choice should be to introduce new bounds that make lifting this limit reasonable, not optimise the reference implementation to mitigate it. In this case, this seems clearly preferable to me:
- The current memory bound can be preserved by introducing a limit on the sum of the size of all stack elements.
- The computation bound can be preserved by restricting hashing operations from operating on elements larger than the current maximum stack element size (in the same fashion as the arithmetic opcodes are currently restricted from operating on elements larger than 4 bytes).

Furthermore, the cache approach here is brittle. It assumes a DoS attacker can’t evade the cache, which can’t be guaranteed in general when inputs are attacker-chosen [^1]. It does hold here, but only indirectly due to restrictions on scripting capabilities for large elements. Such a design would unnecessarily lock us into keeping these restrictions.

[^1]: For instance, this is the reason why Bitcoin Core caches valid signatures but not invalid ones: there is an unbounded number of invalid signatures one can create to evade the cache.

discussion seems spread out, but overall agreement with @darosior 

https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/issues/3#issuecomment-6858912363

I was experimenting a bit with both changes in stage 1 (ref-counting) and stage 2 (hash caching), using some scripts. I think there are some script cases that neither stage addresses.

One example (assuming the stack limit is raised to 6kb) is a script like this:

```
<big_blob (6kb)> IFDUP VERIFY …
```

Both OP_IFDUP and OP_VERIFY scan the element until they find a nonzero byte, so an attacker can push a stack element with the nonzero byte last (5999 zero bytes + 0x01). This forces the interpreter to do 2 full scans of the same shared element for each `IFDUP VERIFY` pair.


> Duplication and hashing cost only a single weight unit in tapscript, with no upper limit on how many times they can be executed, aside from implicit limits due to the 10,000 byte script size maximum.

AFAIK 10,000 byte script size limit you mention in the PR description only applies to legacy and segwit, it doesn't apply to tapscript, so an attacker could produce a script close to the max standard tx weight of 400,000 WU (`MAX_STANDARD_TX_WEIGHT`).

So the script becomes:

```
<stack_element (6kb)> [IFDUP VERIFY] (repeated 180000 times)
```

That's about 366k WU of witness data (180,000 * 2 bytes + 6kb stack bytes).

For a fair comparison, I also scaled your RMD160 script from the PR description up to the same ~366k WU. Since the 10000 byte script limit doesn't apply to tapscript, the worst case in your example could actually be worse than the 4284 RIPEMD160 evaluations you described.

I ran a benchmark on both the 520 and 6000 stack element limits. The results:


| Becnhmark | Element size | 104c7a0288 | Stage1 (40a419af63) | Stage 2 (1d642257b7) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| VerifyDup3HashDropFull_| 520 b | 204.1 ms | 191.8 ms | 14.5 ms *(14x faster)* |
| VerifyDup3HashDropFull_ | 6000 b | 1856.2 ms | 1832.3 ms | 13.7 ms *(135x faster)* |
| VerifyIfDupVerifyLast | 520 b | 83.3 ms | 68.4 ms | 68.6 ms *(no change)* |
| VerifyIfDupVerifyLast | 6000 b | 728.5 ms | 693.3 ms | 689.7 ms *(no change)* |

(Benchmark code on my branch if you wanna take a look https://github.com/jrakibi/bitcoin/commit/9d589117cb92b0d62de19f4196ecc490d2f8b2ad, coming from a Rust background, I might be missing something in the C++ code)

For the repeated hashing case from the PR description, stage 2 makes a big difference: about 14x faster with 520 byte and 135× faster with 6000-byte elements, but the boolean scan gets no improvement from stage2, with the 6kb case still about 10x slower than the 520 byte case even after both stages. (Will open an issue on the SHRINCS repo since I have more stuff to share on that, but I guess boolean scanning is also something that needs to be addressed alongside hash caching and reference counting.)


> I don't think we need be concerned with attacks that push identical elements, because such pushes must be paid for by the attacker in bandwidth and fees.

I believe that with a variant of the case I gave before, an attacker can create a UTXO whose tapscript always fails execution (eg. ends with `OP_FALSE`), and make nodes execute this script each time he tries to spend from it, without ever paying a fee for the spends. Nodes reject the spending tx, but he can submit it again (with a small change to dummy witness data to get a new wtxid) and the node re-runs full script validation each time.

I think this PR is useful to have, but am slightly leaning toward keeping the limit of 520 bytes and using chunking for PQ sig instead. Jonas suggestion here https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/issues/3#issuecomment-4918125246 makes more sense to me: for SHRINCS, we can *always* consume 12 chunks, so the number of elements popped doesn't depend on parsing untrusted data, and keep the size limit as it is. We never know if someone can come up with another opcode combination that isn't covered by the mitigations suggested so far (opcode restrictions, hash caching, ref-counting). The boolean scan above is one example that hash caching and ref-counting don't address.

@jrakibi weird timing, but I said pretty much this at the link above you


edit: note that MAX_STANDARD_TX_WEIGHT isnt consensus, so your numbers are ~10x worse for a one-tx block

Wait, doesn't `elemTrue` introduce cross-core atomic contention in `CCheckQueue`?

With `static const valtype vchTrue(1, 1)`, reads were const and the cache line remained in Shared (S) state across all core caches without bus traffic.

Copying a `std::shared_ptr` executes `lock xaddl` on `_M_use_count`. When parallel script verification evaluates a valid block across 16+ worker threads, almost every standard transaction ends in a successful `CHECKSIG` or `EQUAL`. All worker threads contend on this single control block, bouncing the cache line across sockets and serializing execution. In local benchmarks, multi-threaded throughput degrades by over 2x (Welch test t = -4.86, p = 1.56e-5).

Beyond contention, wrapping elements in `std::shared_ptr` doubles heap allocations on the hot path. Moving a `valtype` into the stack is a 3-pointer transfer, whereas `MakeStackElem` allocates a separate 48-byte control block (`std::make_shared`). Pushing elements becomes ~4x slower (312 ns vs 1310 ns per push).

Since the interpreter stack machine is thread-local, atomic refcounting on `OP_DUP`/`OP_DROP` adds synchronization where no cross-thread sharing exists.

> Could you show how you got those numbers?

The contention was measured in `CCheckQueue` (16 workers) against the static instance prior to `62520cf`. Moving them to locals eliminates the bus lock bouncing, but replaces it with two unconditional heap allocations on every `EvalScript` call before inspecting a single opcode. That allocator churn explains the +38.8% regression in your benchmark.

The larger issue is architectural. The 10KB duplication attack is consensus-invalid today under `MAX_SCRIPT_ELEMENT_SIZE = 520`. Any future soft fork that raises element limits must budget its own hashing costs anyway (analogous to BIP 342 sigops), rather than penalizing existing mainnet script evaluation. Also, pointer identity does not imply data equality. Pushing identical elements separately creates distinct allocations, bypassing a pointer-keyed cache entirely while pinning dropped elements in memory.

> The larger issue is architectural. The 10KB duplication attack is consensus-invalid today under MAX_SCRIPT_ELEMENT_SIZE = 520. Any future soft fork that raises element limits must budget its own hashing costs anyway (analogous to BIP 342 sigops), rather than penalizing existing mainnet script evaluation.

We did consider enforcing new consensus rules as a solution. See [this section](https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/blob/4fe68e3a68fd58be6b0e19436ff6fb7a3357a291/leaf-version-0xC2.mediawiki#user-content-Relaxing_the_Max_Stack_Element_Size). The most obvious option is to merely prohibit duplication or hashing opcodes from executing on inputs larger than today's 520b limit. A more subtle sigops-like budget system is also an option. 

However, we reasoned that additional implementation complexity (pointers and caching) was worth it for a simpler and more permissive consensus rule set, with less arbitrary discontinuities. 

> Also, pointer identity does not imply data equality. Pushing identical elements separately creates distinct allocations, bypassing a pointer-keyed cache entirely while pinning dropped elements in memory.

I don't think we need be concerned with attacks that push identical elements, because such pushes must be paid for by the attacker in bandwidth and fees. We are concerned with duplicate-and-hash attacks which are cheap and asymmetrical to their validation cost.

The cache does not need to guarantee "if we hashed the bytes `0xABCD...` then we never need to hash them again". We only need to guarantee "if a spender pays to push some large stack elements, we only hash each such element at most once". 

Put another way... It's OK if two distinct pointers refer to the same bytes cause two cache misses. What would NOT be OK would be if a pointer is reallocated to store a _different_ byte vector, after a prior cache insertion for that pointer, leading to a cache hit that yields the wrong hash. We prevent this by pinning any such elements' pointers for the duration of script evaluation. For details, see my working branch for stage 2: https://github.com/conduition/bitcoin/compare/scriptvalptr-stage1..scriptvalptr-stage2

This design would break if we had opcodes that allowed users to modify or push large stack elements, such as OP_CAT for example. But under the current script system, it seems robust and simple.
